one_line: Xiaomi AI Cube vs DGX Spark: headline specs measure different things. Batch size, concurrency, serving config and the network decide real throughput; the Cube is still unshipped.
summary: Kai Explains compares Xiaomi's unannounced AI Cube (D100 chip) with NVIDIA's DGX Spark and argues that the viral spec-sheet comparison mixes incompatible measurements. The video walks through five rounds (capacity, memory bandwidth, batch-size throughput, software configuration, multi-node scaling) and ends with buying guidance by workload. Xiaomi's 1.22 TB/s figure applies only to a small pool bonded next to the compute, and its 330 tok/s is a batch-one result on a 3B model, whereas a Spark developer published 1,095 tok/s across 32 concurrent requests on a 27B model. The speaker says his earlier "memory bandwidth decides everything" framing holds only for one machine and one user; above one box, the network fabric sets the ceiling. He also shows a Spark owner gaining roughly 10x from configuration flags, mainly by enabling prefix caching that the serving stack leaves off by default. Verdict: for one user, a used gaming GPU is faster; for parallel agents or a small team, the Spark works as a cheap server; the Cube has no price, date or public runtime yet.
speakers: Host of Kai Explains (not named in the transcript)

key_ideas.idea: The headline numbers in the viral Xiaomi post describe different chips and conditions, so the 330 tok/s vs $4,500 Spark comparison is invalid even though both figures are real.
key_ideas.detail: Each of Xiaomi's five specs belongs to a different component; the speaker sorts them by chip and by measurement condition before any comparison.

key_ideas.idea: Capacity is a gate, and Xiaomi's memory figure is unresolved.
key_ideas.detail: The Spark has a verified 128 GB, in stock at $4,699. Xiaomi's English headlines say 160 GB, but its Chinese copy attaches that to the D100 die ceiling; three readers independently got about 80 GB for the prototype.

key_ideas.idea: The 1.22 TB/s figure is the speed of a small near-memory pool, not the bandwidth serving the large model.
key_ideas.detail: Xiaomi bonds two memory wafers onto the processor face to face at a claimed 1.4 micron pitch (TSMC production stacking about 6 microns, HBM4 about 10). One analyst estimates the pool at 3.5 to 4 GB, which the speaker flags as inference. A 120B model at 4-bit (~60 GB) can't run from that pool, so the demo must have used ordinary memory.

key_ideas.idea: Batch size one is the bandwidth-bound regime; batching changes the picture completely.
key_ideas.detail: Xiaomi's 330 tok/s is a batch-one lab result on its 3B MIMO model. A developer's Spark run on a 27B model published 86 tok/s at 1 concurrent request, 508 at 8 and 1,095 at 32, because one weight read serves all concurrent answers.

key_ideas.idea: Serving-stack defaults can leave a box running at a fraction of its capability.
key_ideas.detail: A Spark owner measured 7.9 tok/s at stock settings on a 27B model. After tuning, the same box hit 58.5 on edit-heavy work and 75 at 4-bit, roughly 10x from flags alone. The main factor was prefix caching, off by default for that model class and not announced at startup; enabling it made shared prompt processing 14 to 22 times faster.

key_ideas.idea: Xiaomi has not published a runtime, so there is nothing to benchmark yet.
key_ideas.detail: No backend in llama.cpp or vLLM, no quantization path and no loading docs. The speaker's signal to watch is an X-ring backend merging into llama.cpp or vLLM; until then he guesses the first customer is a Xiaomi robot.

key_ideas.idea: Above one machine, the network fabric decides performance, and memory bandwidth stops being the ceiling.
key_ideas.detail: A 16-node Spark cluster on a 400 Gb switch runs a frontier-class open model at over 50 tok/s single-stream. Four Sparks reach 124 tok/s on one model where two reach 85. The speaker's earlier framing was corrected: dropping fabric from 200 Gb to 100 Gb cost 2% token generation but 20% prompt processing.

key_ideas.idea: Buy by workload: single-user, parallel agents, or capacity for a small team.
key_ideas.detail: For one person asking one question at a time, a used gaming GPU is 2 to 4x faster on models that fit its VRAM. For parallel agents or a small team, the Spark is an inexpensive server; one buyer estimated about two years to pay back at six concurrent sessions against current API pricing, and never at one request at a time.

techniques.name: Normalize vendor throughput claims before comparing
techniques.how: For each figure, record the chip, model size, precision, batch or concurrency level, and which memory pool it measures. Only compare numbers that match on all of those; mismatched figures get labelled as different products.
techniques.when: Reading or writing any hardware comparison for local inference, or any tokens-per-second claim.

techniques.name: Benchmark a box at several concurrency levels
techniques.how: Run the same model at 1, 8 and 32 concurrent requests and report tok/s per level as a table (the speaker's example: 86, 508, 1,095 tok/s on a 27B model on one Spark). Reading the table shows whether the workload is bandwidth-bound (batch 1) or compute-bound (high batch).
techniques.when: Sizing a local inference box for a team or parallel agents, or deciding whether batching is worth configuring.

techniques.name: Check the serving stack's defaults before judging hardware
techniques.how: Compare stock and tuned runs of the same model (speaker: 7.9 vs 58.5 and 75 tok/s). Look for features that default to off without a startup warning, and prefix caching in particular: enable it when many requests share a prompt prefix (speaker: 14 to 22x faster shared prompt processing).
techniques.when: Benchmarking a local serving stack (vLLM, llama.cpp or similar), or when a box looks slow for its spec.

techniques.name: Test network sensitivity before scaling out
techniques.how: Measure token generation and prompt processing separately while halving the inter-node link speed (speaker: 200 to 100 Gb cost 2% and 20%). Prompt processing is the more fabric-sensitive metric.
techniques.when: Designing a multi-node inference cluster or deciding whether a fabric upgrade is worth it.

techniques.name: Fit check and payback arithmetic for a purchase
techniques.how: Check that the model fits the memory pool it actually runs from (speaker: 120B at 4-bit is about 60 GB, so it cannot run from a 3.5 to 4 GB near-memory pool). Then compare the box's cost against API spend at the expected concurrency: payback at six concurrent sessions was about two years, and never at one request at a time.
techniques.when: Deciding whether to buy a unified-memory box or a GPU for local models versus paying for hosted APIs.

tools: Xiaomi AI Cube (D100 chip, prototype, unannounced)
Xiaomi MIMO (3B model at the batch-one lab result)
X-ring backend (name as spoken in the transcript, unverified)
Xiaomi phone processor (113 GB/s memory bandwidth, not the Cube chip)

numbers.claim: Xiaomi's five headline figures: 200 TOPS, 1.22 TB/s, up to 160 GB unified memory, 150 W, 120B parameters running locally. The post behind it had 743,000 views.
DGX Spark: 128 GB memory, verified, in stock at $4,699.
Xiaomi memory: English headlines say 160 GB; Chinese copy ties it to the D100 die ceiling; three readers got about 80 GB for the prototype.
Bonding pitch 1.4 microns (Xiaomi) vs about 6 microns (TSMC production stacking) vs about 10 microns (HBM4).
Near-memory pool size estimated at 3.5 to 4 GB by one analyst (speaker flags this as inference). A 120B model at 4-bit is about 60 GB.
Xiaomi phone processor memory bandwidth: 113 GB/s (the only published ordinary-memory figure in the family; not the Cube chip). Spark unified memory: 273 GB/s.
Xiaomi 330 tok/s is a batch-one result on a 3B MIMO model. Spark on a 27B model: 86 tok/s (1 request), 508 (8 requests), 1,095 (32 requests).
Spark stock 7.9 tok/s on a 27B model; tuned 58.5 tok/s (edit-heavy) and 75 tok/s at 4-bit, roughly 10x from configuration flags.
Enabling prefix caching made shared prompt processing 14 to 22 times faster.
16-node Spark cluster on a 400 Gb switch runs a frontier-class open model at over 50 tok/s single-stream and about 100 W per box. Another setup has 36 boxes with 4.6 TB unified memory.
Four Sparks on one model: 124 tok/s, vs 85 for two Sparks; six simultaneous conversations at 75 tok/s each.
Fabric 200 Gb to 100 Gb: token generation down 2%, prompt processing down 20%.
Payback about two years at six concurrent sessions vs current API pricing; no payback at one request at a time. Used gaming GPU is 2 to 4x faster for one user on models that fit in VRAM.
Xiaomi's MIMO 2.5 is over 300B parameters; the D100 ceiling is just above 200B. Xiaomi has a public pledge capping hardware margins at 5%. The two chips reach commercial availability in 2027.
NVIDIA raised Spark price by $700 this year because memory got more expensive.

hot_takes: Comparing Xiaomi's 330 tok/s with the $4,500 Spark is an apples-to-oranges comparison; both figures are real but measure different things.
Memory bandwidth decides speed for one machine and one user only; above one box, the network fabric matters more.
The Spark's throughput at high concurrency (1,095 tok/s on a 27B model) is far higher than its batch-one number, so single-stream benchmarks mislead for multi-user workloads.
Xiaomi's first customer for the chip is probably a Xiaomi robot (speaker's guess), and its Cube will probably be cheap (speaker's prediction; cites the 5% margin pledge).
Default serving configurations can leave hardware at a tenth of its capability with no warning (the prefix-caching example).

relevance.why: InferCraft runs vLLM plus Ray Serve on one RTX 5090 with KV-cache strategies and a priority scheduler. The video's batch-size scaling, the prefix-caching default, and the multi-node fabric sensitivity bear directly on that serving layer.
relevance.action: Benchmark the InferCraft vLLM setup at 1, 8 and 32 concurrent requests, report tok/s at each level, and confirm prefix caching is enabled in the serving config.

relevance.why: The video covers local inference hardware and serving stacks, not the Claude Code harness, checkpointing, or approvals.
The normalization checklist (batch size, concurrency, memory pool, fit, payback vs API spend) is a reusable method for judging any local-model hardware or throughput claim.
relevance.action: Add a short checklist for hardware and tokens-per-second claims (chip, model size, precision, concurrency, memory pool, stock vs tuned config) to the team's notes on local AI.
